Unity's new fellowship program offers cash and dedicated support for indie devs
Ten selected developers will receive $50,000 as well as 'resources, support, and networks' for the final leg of their development journey.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
November 16, 2026
schedule
4 Min Read
Image via Unity
Unity
is kicking off
Unite Tokyo
this week with a notable announcement about a new fellowship opportunity for independent game developers using the ubiquitous game engine to ship on games on mobile, console, or PC. Starting today, developers whose games are "roughly a year from launch" can apply to the new "Unity Fellowship," which will select ten indie teams and provide them with dedicated resources to accelerate the last leg of their development journey.
Those resources include a little bit of everything—but most notably, some cold hard cash. The ten selected teams will receive $50,000 that they can spend at their leisure. Unity won't be demanding any equity or repayment. That financial support also comes with a dedicated point-of-contact at Unity, access to a network of industry experts, guarunteed presence at Unity events, and PR and marketing support. Developers interested in landing that support can
apply here
.
Related:
Newly-proposed EU law could place tight restrictions on free-to-play games
In an exclusive interview with GameDeveloper.com, Unity senior vice president of product Adam Smith described the Fellowship as the latest step in its long-running mission of "democratizing" game development. "Regardless of how big or small your studio or your game is, we want to make sure that we're still investing in the democratization of games," he said, noting that the concept of "democratizing" game development is "different" in a world where developers have access to so many tools, and so much content is flooding the marketplace on a daily basis.
"Discoverability—the ability to stand out, to market your game correctly, to make sure that you reach players who are going to be interested in your game—that is going to be one of our key efforts going forward," he added. According to Smith, Unity won't be selecting developers based on the platform they're shipping on, but rather the strength of their creative vision.
Smith said Unity is looking to support games that could be "the next
Valheim
, the next
Hollow Knight: Silksong
, or the next
Among Us
," all successful games made with Unity. Smith said developers might use the $50,000 to acquire testing hardware to help their game launch on as many devices as possible, or to pay for a targeted marketing campaign, or access other kinds of support not covered in the Fellowship's other resources.
He observed that Unity has made huge strides in enabling developers to explore all sorts of unique and creative visions—but a common bottleneck for success comes in the go-to-market stage during what he described as "that last one percent that's actually the last 20 percent of game development."
Related:
Tripwire Interactive lays off workers after announcing new publishing initiative
"Our [goal] is to have that closer relationship with these titles that we really, really want to put put our our initiative behind, so that they can ensure that every obstacle that we know they're going to encounter, we can help them be prepared for it in the most optimal way, and that they can be on the offensive, not in a reactive stance, to overcome all this and have a successful launch on as many platforms as they want."
'We don't succeed unless our community succeeds'
If Unity isn't looking for a return-on-investment in its $50,000 (something even the most generous small lender would seek), what's driving the financial incentive here? "We don't succeed unless our community succeeds," Smith explained. "We don't have a business if they don't have a business, so it behooves us to want to ensure that we're adding as much fuel to their fire as possible."
Keen-eyed industry observers will also be aware that it's not games like
Valheim, Hollow Knight: Silksong,
or
Among Us
that necessarily drove Unity's recent run of
successful quarterly results
. Those were elevated by its mobile advertising infrastructure, which Unity of course pitches as a big incentive for mobile developers (free-to-play and otherwise) to rely on its tools.
Related:
One in three developers say they've been laid off within the last two years
The mobile free-to-play market's is
exceptionally lucrative
—but that profitability comes in an extremely cutthroat environment, where costs of user acquisition are growing beyond many developers' reach. Smith reckons that if Unity mobile developers had the resources to spend on that initial advertising window where interest in a game will be at its highest, they have a better shot at building long-term stability. So there is what he called "shared success" for Unity if those titles take off. He nodded to
Azra Games
'
UnGodly
as a recent example of a mobile game built on Unity that matches this vision.
"But that's not the point," he said. "The point is an investment into studios that we believe in that can help them bring their games to as many players as possible at all. The money is really not the spirit of this—it's more about providing them with a one-to-one relationship [with Unity]."
